newsitem.title: INDIA: Cotton-India prices seen rising on supply shortage.
newsitem.headline: Cotton-India prices seen rising on supply shortage.

text.p: Reduced supplies of cotton due to an indefinite truck strike and improved demand from yarn mills to meet export commitments are expected to keep cotton prices firm in the near term, dealers said on Thursday.
They said the truck strike had affected movement of cotton from production centres to the markets.
Transporters, who pulled their trucks off the road from Tuesday, are demanding the withdrawal of a 5.0 percent service charge and scrapping of a proposed rise in insurance premiums.
Traders said the government's recent decision to allow an additional export of 20 million kg of cotton yarn had cheered market sentiment.
The latest quota takes the total government authorisation of yarn exports in 1996/97 (October/September) to 140 million kgs against 120 million in the previous season.
Traders said the government appeared to prefer exports of value-added items like cotton yarn to raw cotton.

Traders had earlier been expecting a further authorisation of at least 200,000 bales of cotton following an official estimate in February of the 1996/97 crop at 16 million bales, the same as in the previous year.
The government has already authorised an export of 1.2 million bales (one bale is 170 kgs) in the current season against 1.59 bales in 1995/96.
"So far mill demand has been low but now I expect improved buying of cotton by spinning mills," Chandulal Thakkar, a leading cotton trader said.
"Arrivals have also dropped as most of the current season crop has been marketed," Thakkar said.
He said nearly 14.50 million bales of cotton of an estimated crop of 16 million in the 1996/97 crop had been sold.
"I'm expecting a further drop in arrivals in the coming weeks," Thakkar said.
Traders said yarn mills were complaining about the shortage of ready stock while farmers were facing inventory problems.
In the week to Thursday, cotton prices recovered on reduced arrivals despite sluggish demand from mills.

In spot, Bengal-deshi rose 20/30 rupees to 900/940 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) and Punjab saw-ginned 10/60 rupees to 1,560/1,660 rupees per maund. F-414 gained 10/50 rupees to 1,890/1,950 rupees per maund.
Gujarat Kalyan (medium-staple) rose 300/500 rupees to 13,500/13,800 rupees per candy (355.56 kg).
"Prices are looking up and are expected to remain firm," said an official of the East India Cotton Association (EICA), a trade representative body.
